title: Healthy office network
description: 40 seconds of normal office traffic: web browsing, DNS lookups and ARP. Includes realistic noise that must NOT raise alarms: one lost packet in a long download and one mistyped domain name.

title: Slow website - lossy link
description: Three office PCs download from the same web server over a congested link. About 1 in 8 packets is lost and re-sent, which makes pages crawl even though the network looks 'up'.

title: DNS server is down
description: The router's DNS service stopped answering. Users retry lookups and nothing resolves, yet connections made directly to IP addresses still work, which proves the link itself is fine.

title: Two PCs with the same IP
description: A second machine boots with a static IP (192.168.1.50) that another PC already uses. Both answer ARP for it, so connections randomly break. Classic misconfiguration, not an attack.

title: MTU black hole over VPN
description: A VPN link only fits 1400-byte packets. Small requests work, but large data packets vanish and are re-sent forever, the 'page half-loads' problem. A router reports 'packet too big' once.

title: Port scan from inside the LAN
description: Device 192.168.1.66 probes 250 ports on a server in a couple of seconds, finding SSH, HTTP and HTTPS open. This is reconnaissance, the step before an attack.

title: ARP spoofing (man-in-the-middle)
description: An attacker keeps telling the victim 'I am the router' and the router 'I am the victim' every 2 seconds, so all of the victim's traffic flows through the attacker's machine.

title: DNS hijacking
description: When the victim looks up a bank and a shop, a machine on the LAN races a forged answer pointing to itself, arriving before the real DNS server's reply.

title: Rogue DHCP server
description: An unauthorised DHCP server answers new devices faster than the real one and hands out ITSELF as router and DNS server, a stealthy way to intercept every new device.

title: Crashed service + slow server
description: Four PCs keep getting 'connection refused' from an internal app on port 8080 (the service is down), while a remote server answers every request after ~650 ms.
expected: FAULT: service refusing connections + FAULT: high latency

title: Outage AND attack at once (pcapng)
description: The hardest case: DNS is down (a fault) while, at the same time, someone scans a server (an attack). Both look like 'the network is broken'; PacketMedic separates them.
expected: FAULT: DNS failure + ATTACK: port scan

title: Extra DHCP server (misconfig)
description: Someone plugged a home router into the office network. It hands out addresses too, but with the SAME router/DNS settings, so it is a mistake, not an attack. Tests the fault-vs-attack judgement.

title: Hostile DNS names (injection test)
description: DNS lookups for names containing <script> tags, HTML and terminal markup. Proves that untrusted packet data is displayed safely everywhere and never executed.

title: Corrupted / malicious file
description: Valid packets, then random garbage, then a record that claims to be 4 GB long. The tool must not crash or run out of memory; it reports what it could read plus warnings.

title: Fake .pcap (text file)
description: A plain text file renamed to .pcap. It must be rejected up front with a clear message.
